title: The Same News, Twice
subtitle: One office closure, written for the company and written for a friend — and what changes between them.
description: A B2 reading and listening text contrasting formal and informal English through the same piece of news written two ways, with register vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: Register is the part of English that textbooks describe last and employers notice first. It is not politeness, exactly, and it is not vocabulary size. It is the set of choices that tells a reader what kind of relationship you think you are in. The clearest way to see it is to take one piece of news and write it twice.
Here is the formal version — a message from a company to its staff.

Following a review of our regional operations, the Board has taken the decision to close the Bristol office with effect from 31 March. All affected colleagues will be offered a role at the Cardiff site or, where relocation is not practicable, a severance package in line with company policy. Individual consultations will commence next week. We recognise that this announcement will be unwelcome, and we are committed to supporting colleagues throughout the transition.
And here is the same news, sent by one of those colleagues to a friend.

So they're shutting Bristol. End of March. Found out this morning. They're saying everyone can move to Cardiff, which is fine if you don't have kids in school here, and otherwise you take the payout. Meetings start next week, one by one, which I'm not looking forward to. Honestly I saw it coming — nobody's replaced anyone here since last summer.

The facts are identical. Everything else has moved. Look first at the verbs. The formal version prefers nouns where the informal one uses verbs: a decision has been taken rather than they decided, consultations will commence rather than meetings start. This is nominalisation, and its effect is to remove people from sentences. Notice that nobody in the formal version actually does anything — the Board takes a decision, but colleagues are offered, and the announcement will be unwelcome without anyone being said to be unhappy about it.

Then the passive voice, which does the same work. “All affected colleagues will be offered a role” — offered by whom? The sentence declines to say, and that is not laziness; it is the point. Formal institutional writing frequently removes the agent from anything difficult, and once you have noticed the pattern you cannot stop seeing it.

Vocabulary shifts too, and predictably: Latin-derived words move up the register and Anglo-Saxon ones move down. Commence rather than start, terminate rather than end, purchase rather than buy, relocation rather than moving, severance package rather than payout. This is a fairly reliable rule in English, and it is the legacy of the Norman conquest, after which the language of law and administration was French and the language of ordinary life was not.

The informal version is doing things the formal one cannot. It has an opinion — “which is fine if you don't have kids in school here”. It admits a feeling: not looking forward to it. It offers an interpretation the company would never print: nobody has been replaced since last summer. And it uses contractions, sentence fragments and a conversational discourse marker, honestly, to signal that this is one person talking to another rather than an institution addressing a category.

Neither version is better. The formal one is doing a job — it has to be accurate, apply equally to four hundred people, and survive being read by a lawyer. The informal one would be inappropriate from a company and is exactly right between friends. What matters is being able to hear which one a situation calls for, because using the wrong one is the error people actually notice: a job application in the register of a message to a friend reads as careless, and a message to a friend in the register of a company announcement reads as cold, or as though something is being hidden.

vocabulary.definition: the level of formality a piece of language is pitched at
starting on the stated date; a formal fixed phrase
moving to a different place to work or live
able to be done in practice
the money and terms given to an employee who is losing their job
a formal meeting in which someone is asked for their view
to begin — a formal word for start
the period of change from one state to another
an informal word for a lump sum of money paid out
turning a verb into a noun, which removes the person doing the action
a construction in which the thing acted on becomes the subject
the person or thing performing the action in a sentence
to choose not to do something
the older Germanic layer of English vocabulary
something left behind by an earlier period
a shortened form such as don't or they're
an incomplete sentence used deliberately, such as “End of March.”
a word such as honestly or anyway that signals the speaker's attitude

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Read for what each version can and cannot do.

items.prompt: How does the writer define register?
options: The set of choices telling a reader what kind of relationship you think you are in
The size of a writer's vocabulary
The degree of politeness in a message
items.explanation: The definition explicitly rules out both politeness and vocabulary size in the sentence before.

items.prompt: What is nominalisation, and what does it do?
options: Using longer words, which makes writing harder to read
Turning verbs into nouns, which removes people from sentences
items.explanation: “A decision has been taken rather than they decided” — the actor disappears into the noun.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about “All affected colleagues will be offered a role”?
options: It hides who is doing the offering, and that is deliberate rather than careless
It is too vague to be legally binding
items.explanation: “Offered by whom? The sentence declines to say, and that is not laziness; it is the point.”

items.prompt: Why do Latin-derived words sound more formal in English?
options: Because they are longer and harder to pronounce
Because they entered English more recently
Because after the Norman conquest, law and administration used French while ordinary life did not
items.explanation: The text calls the pattern “the legacy of the Norman conquest” — a historical division that still shapes the register.

items.prompt: What can the informal version do that the formal one cannot?
options: Hold an opinion, admit a feeling, and offer an interpretation the company would not print
Reach four hundred people at once
items.explanation: All three are listed, with examples — including the observation that nobody has been replaced since last summer.

items.prompt: What does “honestly” do in the informal message?
options: It signals that this is one person speaking to another rather than an institution to a category
It emphasises that the facts are accurate
It apologises for the bad news
items.explanation: The text groups it with contractions and fragments as markers of a personal relationship.

items.prompt: Why does the writer say neither version is better?
options: Because both contain the same information
Because formality is a matter of personal taste
Because each is doing a different job that the other could not do
items.explanation: The formal one must be accurate, apply to four hundred people and survive a lawyer; the informal one is right between friends.

items.prompt: What error does the writer say people actually notice?
options: Using the register a situation does not call for — which reads as careless, or as cold and evasive
Using vocabulary that is too advanced
items.explanation: Both directions of the error are given, with what each one signals to the reader.

exercises.title: Formal and Informal Pairs
exercises.instructions: Match each formal word to its everyday equivalent.

items.explanation: In almost every pair the formal word comes from Latin or French and the everyday one from Old English — the division the text traces to 1066.

exercises.title: Shifting the Register
exercises.instructions: Complete each formal sentence with the word a company announcement would use.

items.explanation: All three mean the same; only commence fits a formal written announcement.
With effect from is a fixed formal phrase for “starting on”.

items.prompt: Where ___ is not ___, a severance package will be offered.
items.explanation: Both are the formal choices — and note how much less human the sentence is than “if you can't move”.

items.prompt: A decision has been ___ by the Board.
items.explanation: “Take a decision” is the formal collocation, and the nominalisation is what lets the sentence avoid saying they decided.

items.prompt: Staff will ___ ___ a role at the Cardiff site.
items.explanation: The passive removes the agent: nobody is named as doing the offering.

items.prompt: We are ___ to supporting colleagues throughout the ___.
items.explanation: Both are institutional vocabulary. Notice that “committed to supporting” promises less than “we will support”.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: The two versions contain different facts.
items.explanation: False — “the facts are identical. Everything else has moved.”

items.statement: The writer treats the passive voice here as a mistake.
items.explanation: False — removing the agent is “not laziness; it is the point”.

items.statement: The informal version includes an opinion about who the move suits.
items.explanation: True — “which is fine if you don't have kids in school here”.

items.statement: The writer says formal English is generally better writing.
items.explanation: False — “neither version is better”; each is doing a job the other could not.

items.statement: A message to a friend written in company register can read as cold or evasive.
items.explanation: True — “as cold, or as though something is being hidden”.

discussion: “Nobody in the formal version actually does anything.” Find a real announcement and check whether that is true of it.
Is removing the agent from difficult news dishonest, or just professional?
“Committed to supporting” promises less than “we will support”. What other phrases sound like promises without being them?
Which register do you find harder to write in your own second language, and why?
Take the informal message in this text and rewrite it as the formal announcement, then compare yours with the one given. What did you change first?
